This verse closes the passage answering the Meccan unbelievers, who found it strange that revelation should come to Muhammad ﷺ from among them. The commentators explain that they do not own the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, nor the treasuries of divine mercy, and that if they claim such power, let them climb up by the means that reach the sky. The verse then calls them a small, defeated host among the confederates. Most commentators agree that it is a threat and a consolation for the Prophet, and that it recalls the earlier peoples who gathered against their messengers. They also agree that the particle ma is emphatic, expressing either contempt or, in a mocking tone, great importance. They differ on the referent of hunālika. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the battle of Badr, which God had promised while the Prophet was still in Mecca. Ibn 'Atiyya lists other readings: the ascent by the means to heaven, the protection of the idols, or the Battle of the Trench. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as the place where these people took on a lofty claim, and Ibn Kathir links the verse to the defeats that befell the wicked nations. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi understand the confederates as the earlier nations that opposed their prophets, so that the Quraysh are of their kind and are warned by what befell them. Al-Baghawi calls the verse a rebuke and a challenge to their incapacity, and holds that the defeat occurred at Badr as the Prophet had announced.

This verse recalls that the people of Noah, ʿĀd and Pharaoh, lord of the stakes, denied their messengers before the Quraysh, offering consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to the polytheists. The commentators differ on the meaning of Pharaoh's title « lord of the stakes ». Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and ʿAṭāʾ report that he had stakes, ropes and playgrounds where he amused himself. Al-Suddī, Muqātil and al-Kalbī say he tortured people by staking them between four pegs until they died, while al-Ḍaḥḥāk and, in another report, Ibn ʿAbbās understood it as solid buildings. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabarī mainly favour the sense of firm power and enduring rule, a usage found in the verse of al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur. Ibn Qutayba and al-Zamakhsharī note that the root refers to a tent held up by its pegs, an image later applied to sovereignty. On « the people of the Thicket », Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and al-Suddī explain it as a dense grove, and most say it refers to the people of Shuʿayb. The phrase « each of them only denied the messengers » is explained by Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Zamakhsharī as meaning that denying one messenger is denying all, since their call is one. On « a single cry », most identify it with the first blast or a sudden punishment, and « fawāq » can be read with two vowels, meaning return, respite or the interval between two milkings. In « our Lord, hasten for us our qiṭṭ », Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda take it as the punishment threatened to the Prophet, said mockingly; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr sees it as the record of deeds or their share of Paradise; al-Ṭabarī takes it as the good or evil they deserve in this world.

This verse names three peoples of the past who denied their messengers, Thamud, the people of Lot and the people of al-Aykah, and calls them al-ahzab, the factions united in disbelief. Al-Tabari explains al-Aykah as a dense thicket of trees, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala says it is a tangle of sidr and acacia, while most commentators identify these people as the people of Shu'ayb. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri recall that the people of Lot were punished when their cities were overturned, and Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that Thamud perished by the Cry. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi take the words « those » to mean that the defeated factions are exactly those who denied, whereas al-Zamakhshari reads the phrase « they were only denying the messengers » as emphasis: denying one messenger amounts to denying them all, since their call is one. Ibn 'Ashur explains that Pharaoh is mentioned first because his situation resembles that of the leaders of Mecca. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur also point out that the verb takes the feminine form because the word « people » is feminine in sense. Most commentators read the passage as a consolation to the Prophet and a warning to his contemporaries that they may suffer the same fate.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage recalling earlier peoples who denied their prophets, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Pharaoh of the stakes, Thamud, the people of Lut and the companions of the Thicket, whom the Qur'an calls the confederates. The passage consoles the Prophet ﷺ and warns the Quraysh that they may face the same fate. Most hold that denying one messenger amounts to denying all of them, since their message is the same, so the punishment is deserved. The meaning of 'dhu al-awtad' is debated: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Tabari report that Pharaoh had stakes and frames on which he played, al-Suddi says he tortured people by pinning them to stakes, while al-Dahhak, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Qutayba understand it as the firmness of his rule, citing the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur on a kingdom with well-fixed tent pegs. For al-Ayka, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi say it is a thicket, while Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' understands it as dense trees. The phrase 'fahaqqa 'iqab' means that God's punishment was due and befell them. For the next verse, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the 'sayha' as the first blast of the trumpet, or a sudden punishment according to others, and 'fawaq' as a respite or a return, depending on the vocalisation. The verse also records the mocking demand of the unbelievers to hasten their 'qitt', which most interpret as their share of punishment or their record of deeds.

God states that the polytheists of Quraysh are only awaiting a single cry, which most commentators identify as the first blast of the trumpet or the cry of the Hour; some take it to be the second blast, and others a punishment that will destroy them in this world. For most, the phrase "mā lahā min fawāq" means that it will neither return nor be repeated, and no respite will follow it: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada read it as "return", Mujahid as "delay", al-Dahhak as "a second time", and al-Suddi as "recovery". Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fuwaq" with a damma, the rest "fawaq" with a fatha; most philologists treat the two as synonyms, while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' distinguish them, the fatha form meaning respite and the damma form the interval between two milkings of a she-camel. The word "qiṭṭ" is taken by most to mean a lot or a record: according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatada, they were mockingly asking for their punishment to be hastened; according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, their share of Paradise; according to Abu al-'Aliya and al-Kalbi, the register of their deeds. These words are generally understood as ridicule and defiance. God then commands His Prophet to be patient with their words, and reminds him of David, the strong one who often turned back to God, to whom the mountains and birds were subjected, glorifying God with him, and who was given wisdom and decisive speech in judgment.

This verse reports that the idolaters of Quraysh, when warned of punishment, mocked and defied the Prophet, saying: "Our Lord, hasten for us our share [qitt] before the Day of Reckoning." The commentators differ on the meaning of "qitt". Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Suddi, followed by Ibn Kathir, understand it as their portion of punishment, which they ask to be hastened in derision. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and one report from Ibn 'Abbas, take it as the share of Paradise promised to believers, which they mockingly ask to receive now; al-Razi and al-Nasafi also adopt this reading. Abu al-'Aliya and al-Kalbi take it to mean the record of their deeds, linked to the verses of al-Haqqa about receiving the book in the right or left hand, which they ridiculed. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda explain the word as a lot or a document of reward. Al-Tabari judges most correct that they asked for the speedy arrival of whatever good or evil they deserved in this world, as mockery. The commentators broadly agree that the speech was sarcastic and disbelieving. God then commands His Messenger to bear their words patiently and recalls the story of David as consolation.

God commands His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to be patient with what the disbelievers say, and to recall His servant David, who possessed great strength. Most commentators explain "dhu al-ayd" as strength in worship and devotion, following Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid, while others understand physical and military strength, and al-Tabari combines both meanings. As for "awwab", Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it to mean one who turns back repentant from sins, al-Suddi and Qatada as one who glorifies God and obeys Him, and some report that he sought forgiveness whenever he remembered his fault. The commentators note that David fasted every other day and prayed half the night, which clarifies his strength in worship. All agree that the passage consoles the Prophet, reminding him that earlier prophets endured their peoples' harm. Regarding the mountains and birds that worked with David, most report that the mountains glorified God with him at evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered around him; Ibn Kathir notes that al-ishraq refers to the time of duha. Some scholars drew from this verse the legitimacy of the duha prayer, while others held that the glorification is not prayer. On the strengthening of his kingdom, some cite guards and armies, others the awe God placed in people's hearts. Wisdom is understood as prophethood or knowledge and understanding, and decisive speech (fasl al-khitab) as judgment, the rule that the plaintiff must produce evidence and the defendant swears, the formula "amma ba'd", or clear and complete eloquence. Al-Tabari favours keeping all these meanings together without restricting the verse to one.

The verse describes Dawud, God's servant and prophet, as strong in obedience to God and constantly turning back to Him. The commentators explain that the subjection of the mountains means they glorified God together with him when he did so, and that the birds gathered around him to join in this praise. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada report that the mountains echoed his glorification, as Ibn Kathir also relates. Al-Razi understands it as God creating life and speech in the mountains, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean the beauty of his voice resounding in the hills. Al-Shawkani, al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi stress that this glorification is real and known only to God. Regarding the evening and the early morning, most understand the evening as the time from afternoon to night and the early morning as the moment of duha. Several commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, cite this verse as evidence for the recommended duha prayer, as Umm Hani reported. Dawud's firm rule is explained by his guards, the awe he inspired, and the case of the cow. Wisdom is taken as prophethood or understanding, and decisive speech as judgment by evidence and oath, or according to others the phrase 'amma ba'd'.

This verse describes how Allah subjected the birds to David so that they gathered around him and glorified God together with him. Ibn Abbas explained that when David glorified God, the mountains echoed his praise and the birds gathered to him and joined in; this gathering is what the verse calls "assembled". Al-Tabari took the word to mean gathering, while Qatada understood it as subjection. As for "each one of them returned to Him" (or "to him"), al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd read it as obedience and returning to submission, while as-Suddi read it as glorifying God. Al-Samani, al-Baghawi and others allow that the pronoun refers to God, so that David, the mountains and the birds each turns back to Him in glorification. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the present tense of "glorify" shows that the praise was renewed moment by moment, whereas "assembled" is a passive participle because the gathering happened all at once, which better shows God's power. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi see this as a miracle given to David, either through a life and understanding given to the mountains and birds, or through the beauty of his voice echoing in the hills and attracting the birds. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that the morning and evening glorification refers to the late afternoon and to sunrise, and that Ibn Abbas linked the term "ishraq" to the forenoon prayer. The overall meaning is a special favour of God to David, which the Prophet is invited to take as an example of patience.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage consoling the Prophet ﷺ and urging him to endure the taunts of his people, recalling David as a servant granted strength and repentance. Most agree that "We strengthened his kingdom" means reinforcing and securing it, but they differ on the means: al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir and others mention the guards and armies, while al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi take it as the awe God placed in people's hearts, and some combine both. As for "wisdom", some say it is prophethood, others understanding, knowledge of judgment or the Sunna, and Mujahid says justice. "Decisive speech" (fasl al-khitab) is most often reported as judging by evidence from the claimant and an oath from the defendant, as narrated from Ali, Shurayh and Qatada; al-Sha'bi takes it as the phrase "amma ba'd", while az-Zamakhshari, al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as clear speech that leaves no ambiguity. The commentators do not choose among these views and note that the meaning may embrace them all.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ about the two litigants who climbed over the wall of David's (peace be upon him) sanctuary and entered upon him. He was alarmed, but they reassured him that they were two parties who had come to ask him to judge with justice. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir generally report that these two visitors were angels sent to alert David to a fault he had committed, while al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi mention that they may have been men. The commentators agree that the word khasm can denote one, two or more persons, which explains the plural verb. As for the cause of the trial, the reports differ: al-Sudi, al-Kalbi and Muqatil say David wished for the rank of his forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and was tested; others say he took pride in his works or promised unconditional justice. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn al-Arabi and al-Qurtubi reject accounts that impugn his honour, especially those about Uriah's wife, and locate the fault in judging hastily before hearing the other party. Ibn Atiyya notes that the reports are numerous and conflicting. There is agreement on David's repentance, his forgiveness, and the honoured nearness and good return granted him by God. Jurists draw from the passage the permission to judge in the mosque and the prostration of recitation at the words 'he fell down bowing and turned in repentance', on which opinions differ.

The verses tell of two litigants who entered David's sanctuary without permission, frightening him, until they reassured him and presented their dispute, asking for a just judgment without bias. Commentators note that khasm can refer to one or many, and most, such as al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Razi, take the two to be angels in human form, while al-Baghawi and others see two men. Nearly all agree that the complaint about the brother is a parable rather than a real case, and that the request concerns justice. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain that David's fear arose from their entering over the wall and outside the appointed hours. The story of Uriah's wife, reported by many exegetes, is judged by Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi to belong to unreliable Israelite narratives; they prefer the reading that his fault was judging before hearing the other side. All agree that David repented, fell prostrate and turned back to God, was forgiven, and was granted a high station and a good return with his Lord.

This passage recounts the two litigants who came to David, peace be upon him, in his sanctuary. The commentators read its apparent meaning as a parable: one of them says that his brother owns ninety-nine ewes and he owns only one, and that the brother demanded it from him and overpowered him in argument. The word na'ja, ewe, is a common metaphor for a woman, and Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it in that sense. The commentators agree that the two visitors were angels in human form, sent to alert David.

They also agree that David ruled against the first litigant before hearing the second, and that this was his lapse, for which he asked forgiveness, fell prostrate and turned back to God in repentance. On the exact nature of the lapse, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that he went no further than asking to take the ewe; Qatada and al-Hasan see it as a glance or a desire; others point to haste in judgement. Ibn Kathir considers most details of the story to derive from Israelite narratives that are not authentic, and advises reciting it while leaving its knowledge to God. Razi, Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi reject as baseless any accusation of grave sin against a prophet, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that the Qur'an alone is the reliable account.

The passage also teaches that a judge should not rule before hearing both parties, that wrongdoing can occur between partners and relatives, and that repentance and seeking forgiveness raise the servant before God, who forgave David and granted him nearness and a good return.

This verse records David's words after two litigants came before him. He says that the one with ninety-nine ewes has wronged his companion who owned only one, by asking to add it to his own flock, and he adds that many partners oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and these are few. The commentators agree that the ewe stands for a woman and that the khulaṭā' are associates. They also note that the detailed story found in circulation is largely drawn from Israelite narratives, none of which can be reliably traced to the Prophet, so many prefer to limit themselves to the text. After the judgment David understood that he had been tested, asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell prostrate and turned back in repentance. On the nature of the trial, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report several accounts, including a desire for the rank of earlier prophets, and a ruling given before hearing the other party, which al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari mention. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi stress that prophets are protected from grave sins and that attributing a fault to them is contested. Ibn al-Qayyim treats the repentance as a means of spiritual elevation. Regarding the prostration, Abu Hanifa and Malik take it as a prostration of recitation, while al-Shafi'i regards it as a prostration of gratitude.

This verse states that God forgave David his fault and gave him a station of nearness and a good return. Most commentators link it to the story of the two litigants who climbed into his sanctuary: one claimed the single ewe of the other, and David ruled for the plaintiff before hearing the defendant. He was rebuked, asked forgiveness, fell prostrate and turned back to God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the forgiveness covers the fault he sought pardon for, and that zulfa means nearness and honour. Al-Tabari takes it as nearness on the Day of Resurrection, while al-Dahhak understands it as mercy. Ibn Kathir notes that most details of the story come from Israelite narratives, none of which is confirmed by an authentic hadith, and he advises only reciting it. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, by contrast, describe the fault as a minor lapse, such as hasty judgement or leaving the better course, and recall that prophets are protected from major sins. Jurists also differ on the prostration linked to the verse: al-Shafi'i sees it as a prostration of thanks rather than of recitation, while Abu Hanifa holds that bowing takes the place of prostration.

This verse addresses Dawud (David): God made him a khalifa, a steward, on earth and commands him to judge people justly and not to follow his desire, lest it lead him astray from God's path. It then warns that those who stray from this path will face a severe punishment for forgetting the Day of Reckoning. Nearly all commentators agree on the general sense: the kingship given to Dawud carries the duty of fair judgment, and desire is the main cause of straying. They differ on the meaning of khilafa. Al-Tabari and al-Sudi understand it as being granted authority over the land. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that "khalifat Allah" should be used only of a prophet, while later caliphs succeed one another. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain it as royal authority or as succession to earlier prophets, and observe that his status did not change after his repentance. On the meaning of forgetting, al-Tabari and al-Sudi read it as neglect. Ikrima proposes an inversion of the words, so that the punishment is on the Day of Reckoning for abandoning justice. Ibn Kathir and al-Jazairi prefer to read it as abandoning faith in the Day of Reckoning and acting for it. Al-Razi argues that desire turns the soul away from spiritual pleasures, and Ibn al-Qayyim stresses the gravity of the judge's office. Several authors relay the story of Uriah's wife, but Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur reject narrations that would impugn the prophets' infallibility.

God states that He did not create the heavens, the earth and what lies between them in vain or as a game, but with truth and wisdom. Ibn Abbas says the creation was not for reward or punishment in the sense of a purposeless act, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that it was not without a profound purpose: God endowed souls with reason and discernment, then set them before duties whose recompense follows their deeds. Al-Tabari understands that creation was meant for people to obey God's commands and avoid His prohibitions, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see it as creation for worship, followed by gathering for the Day of Judgment. As for the 'assumption of those who disbelieved', most commentators take it to mean denial of resurrection and reckoning; al-Zamakhshari argues this amounts to attributing futility to the Creator, so that their acknowledgment of God as creator becomes an empty acknowledgment. All agree that 'woe' signals severe ruin, though most, including the Jalalayn, identify it as a valley in hell, while others read it as a mere threat. The passage goes on to reject equating believers who do good with corrupters on earth, and the pious with the wicked. Muqatil reports that the Quraysh claimed they would receive in the hereafter what the believers receive, while Ibn Abbas takes the verse as general in scope. Al-Razi draws from it a proof of resurrection, and the passage closes by describing the Qur'an as a blessed book meant to be contemplated so that people of understanding may take heed.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Quran as a Book that God sent down to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, a blessed Book, meaning rich in good and benefit. Its purpose is that people reflect on its verses, that is, consider their meanings and draw out their lessons, and that those of sound intellect remember it, take heed, and act upon it. Al-Tabari holds that both readings, "liyadabbaru" in the third person and "litadabbaru" in the second, are valid: the first refers to his people, the second to the Prophet and his followers. Al-Zamakhshari defines reflection as the thinking that leads to grasping the correct interpretations and fine meanings of the text, and he considers that whoever limits himself to the surface of the recitation gains little. He cites, together with al-Qurtubi, al-Hasan al-Basri's remark that many memorize the letters of the Quran without respecting its limits, so that no trace of it appears in their conduct. Ibn 'Atiyya concludes that slow recitation is preferable, since reflection cannot happen in haste. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir stress that the Quran guides the mind toward sound aims. Al-Razi sees the Quran's blessing in what it secures, namely Paradise and deliverance from the Fire, while most agree that the "people of understanding" are those with sound reason and good judgment. Ibn 'Ashur explains that remembrance is recalling what it matters to know, and that reflection is its prerequisite.

God tells us that He granted David a son, Solomon, and praises him as an excellent servant because he constantly turned back to his Lord through obedience, glorification and repentance. The passage then recounts how sleek, swift horses were displayed to him in the evening, and he became so absorbed in them that he forgot the remembrance of his Lord until the sun was hidden behind the veil. He then ordered them brought back and began to stroke their legs and necks. Commentators differ on this gesture. Al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir understand that he slaughtered them, as a punishment on himself and a means of drawing near to God, and al-Kalbi speaks of a thousand horses, while Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and others hold that he caressed them out of affection without a sword, al-Tabari preferring this view since a prophet would not punish an innocent animal. As for what distracted him, Ali and Qatada identify it as the afternoon prayer, whereas others take the remembrance more generally. Scholars also disagree on whether the pronoun of concealment refers to the sun or to the horses. Some report that God later gave him the wind, which runs at his command, in place of the horses.

This verse, according to the commentators, describes a moment in Solomon's turning back to his Lord: in the late afternoon there were presented to him noble, swift horses that stand on three legs with the fourth raised. Most exegetes report that he became so absorbed in watching them that he missed the afternoon prayer; he then said that he had preferred love of the horses to the remembrance of his Lord, and ordered them brought back and began to pass his hand over their shanks and necks. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'saffanat': al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan take it as horses standing on three legs, while Abu 'Ubayda takes it as horses joining their forelegs. On the number of horses, opinions range from twenty to a thousand. 'Khayr' is taken by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sudi and Qatada to mean the horses, and by Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak to mean wealth. The act of 'mash' is read either as slaying them with the sword to draw near to God, or as a gentle stroking out of affection, the latter preferred by al-Tabari. Al-Razi considers that the pronoun in 'radduha' may refer to the sun, a view most judge weak. Several commentators note that one should keep to the plain wording of the text.

God praises Solomon, son of David, as an excellent servant because he often turned back to his Lord in obedience and repentance. The commentators explain that swift, sturdy horses were displayed before him in the evening, and he became so absorbed in watching them that he missed the afternoon prayer until the sun had set. Full of regret, he said: "I have preferred the love of good things," which most of them take to mean horses, "over the remembrance of my Lord." He ordered the horses brought back and began to pass his hand over their legs and necks. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand this as striking them with the sword, a way of removing what had distracted him from prayer, whereas Ibn Abbas, in a report cited by al-Tabari, takes it as stroking them out of affection, an opinion al-Tabari prefers. Some, such as Ibn Mas'ud, take the pronoun "hidden" to refer to the sun, while Qatada and Ka'b describe the veil as a green mountain surrounding creation, and al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari defend the sun as the subject. The number of horses varies widely in the reports, from twenty to thousands. These details remain debated, but all agree on Solomon's regret at missing the prayer and on the overall meaning of his repentance.

These verses praise Solomon, son of David, as an excellent servant because he often turned back to God in repentance and remembrance. According to most commentators, well-bred horses were displayed to him in the afternoon, al-safinat, standing on three legs with the fourth hoof resting on its tip, and al-jiyad, swift ones. Absorbed in watching them, he let the afternoon prayer pass until the sun set. He then said that he had preferred the love of good, meaning the horses, to the remembrance of his Lord, and ordered them brought back, and began passing his hand over their legs and necks. Commentators differ on what this meant. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayda, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba and most exegetes take it as slaughtering the horses with the sword as an offering to God, permitted in his law; al-Kalbi says that a thousand were reduced to a hundred. Another report from Ibn 'Abbas, followed by al-Tabari, al-Zuhri and Ibn Kaysan, holds that he stroked them out of affection and honour, and al-Tabari preferred this view. Al-Razi and al-Alusi found slaughter the more natural reading, while Ibn Kathir considered that he forgot the prayer without intent. Some held that the pronoun in 'bring them back to me' refers to the sun, a view attributed to 'Ali and widely disputed. Explanations of the trial and the body placed on his throne vary greatly. All agree on the lesson of putting the remembrance of God before attachment to wealth, but differ on the details of what he did.

The commentators treat this verse as the trial of Solomon, the placing of a body upon his throne, and his turning back to God. The majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, hold that the body was a demon who took Solomon's form and sat on his throne for a period, after which Solomon regained his kingdom and repented. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that it may instead have been the half-formed child born when Solomon vowed to visit his wives without saying 'if God wills', citing the hadith of Abu Hurayra in the two Sahihs. The tale of the ring, Sidon and idolatry in Solomon's house is transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi from Wahb ibn Munabbih and others, but al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and Ibn Kathir himself reject it as unbefitting prophethood, while Ibn 'Ashur suggests an idol set up in the houses of his polytheist wives. On the phrase 'none after me', al-Tabari, Qatada and 'Ata' take it as a request that his kingdom not be taken from him as it had been, whereas most read it as a kingdom unmatched after him, which Ibn Kathir finds the more evident sense. All agree that the wind was made gentle at his command, that the jinn were subjected to him for building, diving and chaining rebels, that he was given the choice to give or withhold without reckoning, and that he has nearness and a good return with God.

This verse records Solomon's prayer after his trial: he asks his Lord for forgiveness and for a kingdom that would not be given to anyone after him, acknowledging that God is the Bestower. The commentators agree that the trial (fitna) was a divine test, but they differ on its nature. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit, through Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, that the body placed on his throne was a demon who took his form after Solomon lost his ring; Ibn Kathir notes that these reports are largely drawn from Israelite narratives. Al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and others offer different causes, such as an error in judgment or intimacy with his wives without the reservation of God's will. The hadith of Abu Hurayra in the two Sahihs, in which the Prophet ﷺ recalls this same prayer when he overpowered a jinn, is cited by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir. On the phrase 'not to be fitting for anyone after me', Qatada and Ata ibn Abi Rabah take it as a request that his kingdom not be taken from him in his lifetime, Abu Ubayda reads it as 'no one other than me', and al-Zamakhshari sees it as a request for a miracle confirming his prophethood. Ibn Atiyya and others reject the claim that the request reflects envy, a reading the commentator al-Hajjaj had proposed. The commentators then connect this prayer to the subjection of the winds and the jinn that was granted to him in answer.

The verse describes how God subjected the wind to Solomon, so that it blew gently at his command wherever he wished, and subjected the jinn to him: some who built, some who dived, and others bound in chains. The commentators agree that "rukhaan" means gentle and soft, and that "where it reached" means where he willed. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir also take "rukhaan" to mean obedient, while Mujahid understands it as pleasant and Qatada as swift; Ibn Zayd says it is mild, and al-Hasan says it was neither violent nor slow. Al-Tabari reports that the jinn built altars and statues and brought ornaments from the sea, while the rebellious ones were shackled. On the phrase "this is Our gift, so grant or withhold without reckoning," al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to refer to the kingdom itself, so that he could give or withhold as he chose. Qatada and Muqatil take it to refer to the subjection of the jinn, freeing some and binding others. Ibn Abbas also gives a view that it concerns Solomon's sexual potency, which many commentators reject. Several scholars agree that he has a high station with God in the Hereafter. The accounts of the trial that befell Solomon and the body placed upon his throne differ greatly, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that many of these reports come from Israelite narratives.

The commentaries explain this verse as describing the unique authority God gave Solomon over the jinn: some of them served him as builders who made sanctuaries, statues, troughs and great cooking pots, others dove into the sea to bring up pearls, and others, rebellious ones, were bound in chains. The exegetes agree that building and diving were among their tasks and that this subjection was a special gift to him. Most take the 'others' to be rebellious demons, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees them as craftsmen chained so they would not flee. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi note that most of the detailed stories about Solomon's trial and the demon who took his form come from Israelite narratives, which they consider incompatible with prophetic dignity. Al-Razi, by contrast, affirms the real strength of the jinn. Ibn Juzayy explains that 'this is Our gift' refers to the kingdom granted. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi adopt this reading: the kingdom is the gift, and the freedom to give or withhold without reckoning is a favour. Al-Hasan says Solomon was never held to account for any blessing. Al-Tabari reports other interpretations of 'grant or withhold', some tied to marital relations, which most exegetes regard as weakly supported. On 'without reckoning', the majority take it to mean without accountability or limit. The verse closes by affirming his high nearness to God and his excellent return.

In this verse God recounts among the favours bestowed on Solomon that He subjected to him a group of demons bound in chains and fetters. Nearly all commentators understand them to be the rebellious devils, whom Solomon kept shackled to restrain their harm. The verse is read as a continuation of the subjection of the wind and the devils, who were put at his service either to build and dive or to be bound as punishment for their rebellion. The commentators explain that al-asfad means the shackles and fetters, and that the word sifd, meaning a fetter, also came to mean a gift because it binds the one who receives it. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the devils worked for him in construction, crafts and the diving for pearls, and that some of them were chained. As for the word muqarranin, some take it to mean that several of them were tied together, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the shackling as a disciplinary measure to prevent corruption. The commentators go no further in explaining the precise reason for their chaining, and Ibn 'Ashur only emphasises the extent of Solomon's authority. The scene thus highlights the power granted to him and the distinction between obedient and rebellious devils.

The commentators explain that "This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without reckoning" most often refers to the vast kingdom Solomon had asked for, including his command over the wind and the jinn. He is told he may dispose of this power as he wishes without being held to account. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya follow this reading. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take the gift to be kingship itself, so that "famnun" means give and "amsik" means withhold. Qatada and al-Suddi understand it as the jinn: Solomon could free whom he pleased and bind the others. A report from Ikrima attributed to Ibn Abbas takes it as Solomon's sexual capacity, but Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan judge this unreliable, since the verse makes no mention of women. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note the unrestricted generosity the phrase conveys. Ibn al-Qayyim contrasts the king-prophet, who acts under broad delegation, with the servant-prophet the Prophet ﷺ chose. As for "without reckoning", some take it to mean abundance beyond counting, others the absence of accountability in the Hereafter. The verse ends by affirming Solomon's nearness to God and his excellent final return, placing his reward in the afterlife beyond what he received in this world.

This part of the verse tells us that God has reserved for Solomon a station of nearness to Him and a good final return in the Hereafter. The commentators link it to the favours he received in this world: an unmatched kingdom, the wind and the jinn placed under his command. Al-Tabari explains that nearness (zulfa) is the favour owed to his repentance, his turning back to God and his obedience, and that a good return (husn al-ma'ab) means a good destination in the afterlife, a view Qatada also holds. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Sa'di read it as a reminder that what Solomon was given in this world does not lower his rank with God. Ibn al-Jawzi understands nearness as elevated status and dignity. On this general meaning the commentators agree. They differ over the stories told about Solomon's trial, many of which come from Israelite narratives. Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Uthaymin dispute their reliability, while others report them without deciding. Al-Shawkani, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi connect the nearness to both this world and the next without preferring one over the other.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to recall His servant Ayyub when he called out to his Lord that Satan had afflicted him with hardship and torment, meaning distress in his body and trial in his wealth and family. The commentators relate that God answered him and told him to strike the ground with his foot, whereupon a spring gushed forth in which he bathed and drank, and his ailment left him both outwardly and inwardly. God restored his family and gave him as many again, as a mercy and a reminder for people of understanding. The scholars differ on how the affliction is ascribed to Satan. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir see it as a trial willed by God, with Satan acting through whisperings or by God's permission, while al-Razi holds that Satan has no power over illness and that his role was only to cast evil thoughts. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur report several accounts of the cause of the trial, such as anger toward his wife or failing a neighbour or an oppressed man, though these are not unanimously accepted. All agree that God commanded him to strike his wife once with a bundle of a hundred twigs so that he would keep his oath, and praised him for his patience and for being one who constantly turns back to God. The readings of the word nasb vary in vowels, and Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya regard them as having one meaning, hardship and weariness. The commentators do not settle the details of the causes, leaving the manner of the matter to God's knowledge.

The verse recalls Ayyub crying out to his Lord that Satan had touched him with hardship and suffering. The commentators explain nusb as fatigue and harm and 'adhab as pain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report, following Qatada and Muqatil, that the first concerned his body and the second his wealth, while al-Mawardi notes other views treating them as one and the same affliction. God then tells him to strike the ground with his foot, and a spring of cool water gushes forth; he washes in it and drinks, and every illness within and without leaves him. Al-Hasan speaks of two strikes and two springs, one for bathing and one for drinking. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir place these springs at al-Jabiya in Syria, according to Qatada, and al-Mawardi also records Muqatil's view that mughtasal means the place of bathing rather than the water.

All agree that God restored his family and gave him as many again, but they differ on how. Al-Hasan holds that they were brought back to life after dying; Ibn Abbas that they were returned alive and that he was given a like number more; al-Dahhak that none of the dead came back and that new children were born to him. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan add that he was commanded to strike his wife with a bundle of a hundred twigs, fulfilling an oath made during his illness. The reasons for that oath vary: Ibn Abbas mentions a false physician sent by Satan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab an excess of bread, and Yahya ibn Salam a goat to be sacrificed. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi find many of these accounts unreliable, Mujahid limits the concession to Ayyub alone, while Qatada and Ibn Abbas extend it to all believers.

This verse says that Allah gave Ayyub his family and an equal number again with them, as a mercy from Him and a reminder for people of understanding. The commentators differ on the meaning of the gift. Al-Hasan and Qatada hold that Allah revived his family members and doubled them, while Ibn Abbas says He returned them as they were and gave him others like them. Al-Suddi holds that their rewards were restored to him in Paradise, and al-Dahhak that none of the dead returned and that his wife bore him many children. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur explain that his family had withdrawn from him during his illness and later came back after his recovery, while al-Razi considers that God granted him health, wealth and a large offspring. All agree that the gift is a mercy and a lesson that patience leads to relief.

The passage then recalls Ayyub's oath to beat his wife a hundred times. God commanded him to take a bundle containing a hundred stalks and strike her once with it, so that he would keep his oath. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-'Arabi and Ibn Juzayy note that some scholars consider this concession specific to Ayyub and others general. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i accept that one blow suffices, while Malik and his companions require the full number. The commentators also differ on the reason for the oath and on the precise nature of the trial that befell the prophet.

This passage of Surah Sad tells that after Ayyub (Job) was healed, God commanded him to take a bundle of twigs or stalks containing a hundred strands and strike his wife once with it, so that he would fulfil his oath to beat her a hundred times without breaking it. The commentators report that he swore this in anger, over a lapse or an action of his wife, which some link to a temptation by the devil, although she had served him faithfully during his affliction. They all praise Ayyub for his patience under trial and his constant return to God, and they regard his complaint made to God as not contradicting patience. The jurists differ on the scope of this concession: al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa hold that it applies to oaths in general, while Malik considers it specific to Ayyub, as does Mujahid, whereas 'Ata' considers it general. On the nature of the bundle, Ibn 'Abbas speaks of a palm-frond cluster, Mujahid of tamarisk, and others of a handful of grass or stalks. Regarding his family, opinions differ: some say God restored them to life, others that He gave him offspring equal to them. Some scholars drew from this passage the permissibility of certain legal stratagems, while others rejected this, arguing that Ayyub's story does not establish it.

God commands His Prophet to remember His servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom the commentators describe as possessed of strength in worship and insight into the religion. The reading differs between the plural 'ibadana' and the singular 'abdana': most hold that Abraham and his descendants are an apposition or substitute for 'servants', while Ibn Kathir takes Abraham alone as the referent and attaches the other two to him. As for 'the hands' (al-ayd), many early scholars explain it as strength in obedience or in God's cause, while others take it as blessings or good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as a metaphor for actions, and 'the eyes' as understanding. Al-Tabari suggests that the hands may mean the good works they sent ahead to God. On 'purified by a sincere remembrance of the abode' the views vary: some say they were devoted to recalling the Hereafter, warning and renouncing the world; others that love of the world was removed from their hearts; others that they received the finest part of the Hereafter. Nafi' reads 'khalisati dhikra' with an annexed form, others with tanwin, and opinions differ on whether 'the abode' is the Hereafter or this world. The commentators agree that they are among the chosen and the best, that this remembrance is a noble mention of them, and that the righteous will have a fine return in the gardens of Eden.

This verse says that God singled out Abraham, Isaac and Jacob with a pure and unmixed quality: the remembrance of the Abode. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi, agree that God removed from their hearts love of the world and its remembrance, so that their concern was the Hereafter alone, and that they reminded people of it and called them to obey God. Qatada and Ibn Zayd emphasize the call to the Hereafter, while Mujahid and al-Suddi understand it as their fear of the next life and their works done for it. On the reading with the annexed form, khalisat dhikra al-dar, al-Zamakhshari takes the remembrance of the Abode to be free of any admixture, and al-Razi notes that such remembrance may be directed toward God or toward something else. Another view, held by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Jubba'i, Abu Muslim and, as a possibility, Ibn 'Atiyya, takes the Abode to mean this world, and its remembrance to mean a lasting good reputation and praise left behind on earth. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari then link their election to their goodness: they were chosen from among their kind and counted among the righteous. None of the commentators decides between these readings, and al-Tabari holds that each is valid according to the recitation adopted.

In these verses God tells us that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom He describes as possessing strength in His worship and insight into His religion, were singled out for a great distinction: the remembrance of the abode of the Hereafter and working for it. The commentators agree that they laboured for the next life and reminded people of it and of God, and that they are with God among the chosen and the best. On the meaning of "hands", Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as strength in obedience and worship, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand blessings or good deeds, and al-Tabari takes the "sight" as insight of the heart into religion and the "hands" as good deeds sent ahead to God. The explanation of the sincere remembrance varies: Malik ibn Dinar says God removed from their hearts love of this world and its mention; Qatada says they called people to the Hereafter; Mujahid says they had no concern but it; Ibn Zayd says God gave them the best of what is in the Hereafter. On recitation, Nafi' reads "sincere remembrance" with an annexed genitive, while most readers use tanwin, and al-Tabari considers both widely transmitted. The commentators note that "mustafayn" means chosen, and that "akhyar" is the plural of "khayyir" or "khayr". These verses are followed by the mention of Isma'il, al-Yasa' and Dhu al-Kifl, then the gardens of Eden promised to the righteous and the fate of the transgressors.

The verse tells the Prophet to remember Isma'il, al-Yasa' and Dhu al-Kifl, who are among the chosen and the good. Al-Tabari explains that he should follow their example of patience and determination in obeying God and conveying the message, while al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir present the mention of them as an honour and a lasting good name. Most commentators agree that the stories of these men have already been told elsewhere in the Qur'an, so they need not be repeated, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note. The word kifl is glossed by al-Tabari as share or fortune. Opinions differ on Dhu al-Kifl: al-Qurtubi and others treat him as a prophet, whereas al-Shinqiti reports that some regard him as a righteous man who undertook duties and fulfilled them, without a firm ruling by himself. On the linguistic side, the readings of al-Yasa' differ over the presence of the definite article; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain it as an added or definite particle attached to a foreign name. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi note that the phrase "this is a reminder" may refer to the praise given to these prophets or to the Qur'an itself. The God-fearing will have a good return, the Gardens of Eden with their gates open, as the commentators conclude.

The commentators explain that "This is a reminder" refers, in the most common reading, to what precedes in the chapter about the prophets: it is an honour and a good name that will remain for them, as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir report. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan see instead a kind of reminder and a transition to a new theme, the Garden and the Fire, comparing it to how an author moves from one chapter to another. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur also allow that the term may refer to the whole Qur'an, Ibn 'Ashur stressing the sense of an exhortation to follow the prophets.

There is broad agreement that the "good return" (husn ma'ab) is the excellent final destination of the God-fearing in the afterlife. Al-Tabari and al-Suddi understand it as the place of return and destiny, and the commentators specify that this is Paradise. The "Gardens of Eden" are, according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, abodes of lasting residence. Ibn Kathir cites a report describing a palace called Eden, though he himself notes that its chain is weak. On the grammar of "its gates being opened", the Kufans and Basrans differ, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the opening happens by command, which explains the participle rather than "closed".

The commentators agree that the people of Paradise recline, ask for abundant fruit and drink, and have companions of restrained gaze who are of the same age, with Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada differing only in detail. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that this bliss is permanent and never runs out.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the excellent place of return prepared for the God-fearing: gardens of lasting abode, with their gates opened for them. Grammarians debated the construction of "the gates" and the implied pronoun in "opened". Al-Farra' and the Kufans hold that the sense is "opened for them, their gates", the definite article standing in for the pronoun, while the Basrans supply "the gates of them". Al-Zamakhshari treats the gates as an appositive of inclusion. On the meaning of the opening, al-Hasan reports that the gates are addressed and open at command, while others say the angels open them. All agree that this bounty is everlasting: the residents recline on couches, call for abundant fruit and drink, and have beside them spouses who look only to their husbands and are of the same age. Ibn Kathir cites a report of a palace called Adn, reserved for prophets, the truthful, martyrs and just leaders, though he regards its chain as weak. On the word Adn, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean a lasting dwelling, while al-Alusi notes that some treat it as a proper name. As for the opening "this is a reminder", some read it as praise and honour, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur see a mere shift in the discourse or an allusion to the Qur'an itself.

This verse describes the state of the people of Paradise in the Gardens of Eden, whose gates are opened for them. They recline there on adorned couches and call for the abundant fruit and drink they desire, which is brought to them as they wish. The commentators explain that mentioning fruit and drink without food suggests that their eating and drinking are for pleasure and enjoyment rather than to meet a need, as in this world. According to them, the abundance of fruit refers both to its variety and to the quantity of each kind. All agree that this bliss is everlasting and never ends. Al-Tabari reports that the gates open by God's command without anyone pushing them, and al-Hasan says they open when addressed. Ibn Kathir and others understand reclining as sitting comfortably, cross-legged, on couches beneath canopies. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see the word as a circumstantial phrase placed before its verb to keep the rhyme, and the calling for fruit as an independent clause describing their condition. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that this scene gives the God-fearing a promise of peace, tranquility and full delight awaiting them.

This verse describes what God has prepared for the righteous in Paradise: with them are wives who restrain their gaze to their husbands and look at no one else, and who are of the same age. The commentators agree on the basic meaning of 'restraining the gaze': these women do not turn their eyes toward anyone other than their spouses. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi add that this includes their hearts and hearing as well, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi limit it to the gaze. On the word 'atrab', opinions differ. Mujahid and Ibn Abbas understand it as equals in age, Qatada as sharing one age, and al-Qurtubi reports that they are about thirty-three years old. Al-Mawardi lists several readings, including that they are companions who do not hate or envy one another, a view transmitted from Mujahid, and that they are matched to their husbands' ages, a view adopted by Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur explain that this equality removes jealousy. Al-Alusi notes that the description may refer to the wives among themselves or to them and their husbands, and he finds it hard to decide. Finally, the verse ends by affirming that this provision never runs out, a point all the commentators take as its conclusion.

The plain meaning of the verse is that the delights just described, the gardens, the fruits, the drinks and the spouses, are what the pious have been promised for the Day of Reckoning, and that this is a provision from God which never runs out or perishes. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya, agree that the demonstrative refers to the blessings of Paradise mentioned before, reserved for those who are mindful of God as a reward for their good deeds. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that "no end to it" means that these blessings are lasting and uninterrupted, as in the verse about a gift that is never cut off. Al-Tabari, citing al-Suddi, adds that the provision of Paradise renews itself: whenever something is taken from it, a like of it returns in its place, unlike the goods of this world, which are used up.

As for the phrase "for the Day of Reckoning", Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with the third person, "what is promised", while the other readers used the second person, "what you are promised". Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see this shift of address as a mark of honour for the believers. The commentators differ on the meaning of the preposition. Most, such as al-Nasafi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, take it as indicating purpose, meaning for the day on which every soul is repaid for what it did. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Ashur see it rather as indicating a time, or as linking the reward to the reckoning of deeds, and al-Alusi notes that the reward follows from the reckoning. The commentators set out these readings without choosing between them.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the description of the bounties of the righteous in Paradise: what God gives them, fruits, drink and wives who restrain their gaze, is a provision from Him that never runs out or ends. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain nafad as cessation and passing away. Al-Tabari, quoting al-Suddi and Qatada, adds that the provision of Paradise renews itself: whenever a fruit is picked, another like it grows in its place, unlike the goods of this world, which are exhausted.

The commentators agree that rizq here means a gift or favour, and that nafad means end or depletion. Ibn Abi Hatim and later exegetes stress the permanence of this bounty. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir support the point with parallel Qur'anic verses, such as the promise of a gift that is never cut off, and the statement that what is with God endures.

On the reference of the word "this", al-Razi and al-Qurtubi link it to the whole list of blessings just mentioned. The grammarians differ on its role: al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss whether the clause is a circumstantial phrase qualifying rizq or a second predicate of inna, while the Jalalayn accept both readings. Ibn Ashur notes that the demonstrative is used to draw attention, and that the Prophet himself once called a child a provision.

In short, the commentators agree that the verse affirms the enduring nature of God's favour in Paradise, while their differences concern grammar and how the renewal of these goods should be described.

The commentators explain that this verse completes the description of the end of the righteous by setting against it the fate of the transgressors, those who exceeded all bounds in disbelief, disobedience and rebellion against God. They will have the worst return, Hell, where they will burn, and a dreadful resting place. The following verses detail what they will taste: a boiling liquid and a ghassaq, along with other punishments of the same kind. The commentators agree that the hamim is water heated to its utmost heat, and that the ghassaq is what flows from the pus of the damned. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that it is pus, tears, or a fluid oozing from their skins, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil describe it as an extreme cold, and others as an intolerable stench, supported by a hadith of Abu Sa'id cited by Ibn Kathir. On the reading of the word, the linguists hold that the two forms have close or somewhat different meanings. As for the 'other punishments of its kind', Ibn Mas'ud identifies them with zamharir, while al-Hasan and al-Suddi take them to be varied kinds of torment, and al-Tabari prefers the singular reading. The verses then describe the dispute in the Fire: a newly arriving group is greeted with reproach by those who went before, who answer that their leaders led them to this fate, and ask for a double punishment for them. The damned also wonder about men they once considered wicked in this world. The commentators conclude that this quarrel is a certain truth.

This verse states that the fate of the rebellious, those who transgressed against God, is Hell, where they will burn, and that their bed there is a wretched one. The commentators agree on this general meaning, but they differ on the word ghassaq. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Muqatil take it to mean an intense cold that cannot be endured, while Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, 'Ata' and Ka'b al-Ahbar understand it as the pus, blood and tears that flow from the bodies of the damned. Al-Tabari adds that it may also mean a foul stench, relying on a hadith transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Al-Farra' proposed that the words are in reverse order, meaning that this is boiling water and ghassaq, so let them taste it. The readings also differ on the spelling of this word, and on whether «wa-akhar» is singular or plural; al-Tabari preferred the singular, while Ibn 'Atiyya accepted the plural reading. As for «min shaklihi azwaj», Ibn Kathir and al-Hasan read it as other kinds of punishment, while Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas identify it with zemhrir, the bitter cold. The passage then describes the dispute between the misguided leaders and their followers in the Fire: the leaders are greeted without welcome, the followers ask that the punishment of those who led them astray be doubled. The damned also wonder why they do not see the poor believers whom they used to mock, asking whether they were in fact mistaken about them or whether their sight simply failed them.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the fate of the tyrants, those who transgressed the limits in disbelief and disobedience. Their destination is Hell, a wretched bed they prepared for themselves. They are told to taste it: boiling water of extreme heat (hamim) and ghassaq. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the hamim is scalding water of intense heat. The views on the ghassaq, however, differ widely. Al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take it to be the pus and blood flowing from their bodies, or the tears from their eyes. Mujahid and Muqatil take it to be an unbearable, intense cold, and Ibn Abbas associates it with the zamharir, the extreme cold. Al-Zamakhshari notes it may burn by its cold as the hamim burns by its heat. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite a hadith from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that a bucket of ghassaq poured out in this world would stink its inhabitants; al-Tabari uses it as evidence for those who take it to be foul-smelling. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi ultimately favour the view that it is a flowing discharge from their bodies. As for 'and other torments of its kind, in pairs', Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas understand it as the zamharir, al-Hasan as torments unknown in this world, and others as various kinds of punishment. The following verses describe a host rushing into the Fire with their followers; the leaders curse the newcomers, and the followers reply that it is the leaders who brought this fate upon them, then ask God to double the punishment of whoever misled them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy identify this host as the followers, while al-Mawardi and al-Razi also consider the speakers to be the angels or the damned addressing one another. Finally, the damned wonder why they cannot see the men they once considered wicked, asking whether they mocked them or whether their eyes turned away from them. The commentators affirm that this mutual dispute of the damned is an undeniable truth.

This verse, within the description of the fate of the transgressors after that of the righteous, states that the damned will suffer another punishment of the same kind as the boiling water and the ghassaq already mentioned, and that it comes in varied forms and kinds. The commentators agree that the 'tāghūn' are those who rebel against God and deny His messengers, and that the general meaning is a manifold punishment, similar in severity and horror to what precedes it.

They differ, however, on the identity of this additional punishment. Al-Suddi and Ibn Mas'ud hold that it is the zamharir, the extreme cold; al-Hasan considers it a torment never seen in this world; Ibn Kathir lists extreme cold, scorching winds, drinking boiling water and eating the zaqqum tree, while al-Tabari keeps to the general sense of various torments without specifying them.

The readings also differ. The majority read 'wa-akharu' in the singular, while Abu 'Amr and others read 'wa-ukharu' in the plural; al-Tabari prefers the singular for its grammatical soundness, whereas Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim favour the plural because it agrees with 'azwaj'. As for 'min shaklihi', some take it to mean 'of a like nature' and others 'of the same kind'. Finally, the grammarians debate the syntactic role of 'wa-akharu' and 'azwaj', depending on which of the two serves as subject or predicate.

This verse from Surah Sad describes the quarrel among the people of the Fire. The commentators explain that when a new group of followers enters Hell, the keepers say to the leaders: this is a crowd rushing in with you. The leaders reply that there is no welcome for them, for they are destined for the Fire. The followers answer that the leaders deserve that curse more, since they brought them to this fate by misleading them and urging them to disbelief. Commentators agree that marhaban comes from spaciousness, so that la marhaba is a curse of cramped discomfort. They differ on who speaks. Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the keepers of Hell or some of the damned speak, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan also allow that the leaders are speaking among themselves about their followers, and Abu Hayyan prefers this reading. As for the first group, al-Hasan says they are the children of Iblis, others say the leaders, and al-Naqqash identifies them with the Quraysh leaders at Badr. All agree that the tyrants are disbelievers, though al-Jubba'i includes those guilty of major sins. For the request of doubled punishment, Ibn Mas'ud takes the extra torment to be serpents and vipers, while al-Razi explains it as the punishment of misguidance plus that of misguiding others. All affirm that this mutual accusation among the damned is a certain truth.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of the fate of the tyrants, those who transgressed the limits in disbelief and disobedience: their destination is Hell, where they burn and whose bed they have prepared for themselves. The verses then describe what they will taste there: scalding water (hamim) and a purulent liquid (ghassaq). Most commentators agree that hamim is water heated to extreme heat, and that ghassaq is the pus, blood or tears of the damned. Ibn Abbas and al-Zamakhshari also report that ghassaq may mean intense cold, while Ka'b al-Ahbar describes it as a spring in Hell where the venom of serpents and scorpions gathers; al-Tabari and others cite a hadith of the Prophet on its stench. On the readings, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi note that both the short and the doubled forms are transmitted, and al-Tabari favours the meaning of pus. Ibn Kathir and others take "other punishments of its kind" to mean various types of torment; al-Hasan describes them as torments unknown in this world, and Ibn Mas'ud identifies them with zamharir, extreme cold. Then the damned exchange words: the followers greet the leaders with "no welcome for you", and the leaders reply that the responsibility is theirs, since they brought this punishment upon them by misleading them. For most commentators, the prayer for a double torment is directed by the followers against the leaders; al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd attribute it to all the damned. Finally, the disbelievers wonder about men they used to regard as wicked and cannot see, which Mujahid links to the poor believers such as Ammar, Bilal and Suhayb.

This verse records the plea of the followers in Hell, who ask God to double the punishment of whoever set this path for them and made it attractive. Most commentators understand the "tyrants" to be disbelievers who exceed all bounds, while al-Jubba'i holds that the term also covers those guilty of grave sins. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "whoever set this before us" is the one who established and prescribed this way, whereas Muqatil takes it to mean the one who made it attractive. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the plea may come from all the inhabitants of Hell or from the followers alone. The commentators agree that "double" means that an equal punishment is added to the first; Ibn Mas'ud identifies it with serpents and vipers. Ibn Juzayy compares it to the plea in Surat al-A'raf: "Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." Abu Hayyan, al-Zamakhshari and others observe that the exchange contains mutual reproach: the followers answer the leaders that it was they who brought this punishment upon them by misleading them. Readers differ on the phrase "did we take them for mockery": Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it as a statement, while others read it as a question; al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi describe both readings without preferring one. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim add that the followers may curse their leaders, or that all of Hell's inhabitants may call down a double punishment on the devils who instituted polytheism. The commentators conclude that this mutual dispute is a certain truth.

This verse records what the disbelievers in the Fire will say when they look for men they used to regard as wicked in this world and cannot see them. The commentators widely agree that these men were most often poor believers such as 'Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal, Salman and Khabbab, whom the leaders of Mecca looked down on for their poverty and for opposing the religion of their people. Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas say the speakers were Abu Jahl and his companions, while Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Ashur and others widen the address to any disbeliever who sees believers as evil. Readers differ on "atakhadhnahum": some read it as a statement, others as a rebuking question. On "sikhriyyan" some read the form meaning enslavement, others the form meaning mockery. The commentators give two main readings of the sense: either they mocked the believers wrongly in this world, or the believers are in the Fire with them but the disbelievers' eyes do not catch them. Al-Hasan holds that both happened, while Ibn Kathir sees a sign of their self-consolation through absurdity. All connect the verse to the dispute among the people of the Fire, which the commentators affirm as a certain truth.

This passage recounts the dialogue among the people of the Fire. The wrongdoers, now in Hell, wonder why they cannot see the men they once considered wicked in this world, and ask whether their contempt and mockery toward them was a mistake, or whether these men are with them there but their eyes fail to see them. Most commentators identify the wrongdoers as Abu Jahl and his peers among the chiefs of Quraysh, and the men they despised as the poor believers such as Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal and Salman, as al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Nasafi and others state. The reading of «ittakhadhnahum» differs: some read it with a connected alif as a statement describing «rijalan», while others read it with an interrogative hamza expressing reproach and astonishment. Al-Tabari, al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi prefer the first reading because the question has already been asked, while al-Farra' and al-Nasafi take the interrogative form as self-reproach. On «am zaghat al-absar», Mujahid explains it as their error, which kept them from knowing where those men were; al-Hasan sees it as the scornful dismissal of them; and Ibn Kaysan suggests that perhaps those men were better than they were. Finally, the words «Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire» are understood by most commentators as affirming the certainty of these disputes and mutual curses, in which leaders and followers blame one another.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of what the people of the Fire say to one another, and affirms that such exchanges will certainly take place. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the quarrelling as the mutual cursing and disavowal: the leaders say "No welcome for them" about the believers, and the followers reply "Rather, it is you who are not welcome". Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that this exchange is called a dispute because it resembles a contest between adversaries, while al-Alusi and al-Qasimi stress that the blame runs in both directions. Grammarians differ on the parsing of "quarrelling": Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as an apposition to "true", al-Zamakhshari as a qualifier of "that", and Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir as a predicate or apposition. Some hold that all these words come from the damned, others that the statement "No welcome for them" is spoken by the guardians of the Fire. The verse is also read as confirming what precedes it, namely the unbelievers' remarks about the poor believers such as Ammar, Suhayb and Bilal, whom they search for in the Fire without finding them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur add that the phrase emphasises the certainty of these disputes.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to the Meccan polytheists that he is only a warner who cautions them about Allah's punishment for their disbelief, and that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, the One, the Subduer. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it that the Prophet's role is to warn and that pure monotheism is the foundation of his message. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress that the true religion is the oneness of God without peer or partner, and that His might makes Him unconquerable in punishing the disobedient while He is also forgiving to whoever turns to Him. Al-Razi links oneness to dominion: two equal powers could not both be divine, and forgiveness following might gives hope. The commentators agree that the names al-'Aziz and al-Ghaffar combine majesty and mercy. As for the following words, 'It is a mighty tidings', most identify it with the Quran, while others take it to mean the Resurrection, monotheism or prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir explain the dispute of the exalted assembly as the angels' debate about creating Adam, and al-Qurtubi cites the dream hadith about expiations and degrees, noting its chain of transmission. Readers also differ on 'a-ttakhadhnahum' and on whether 'sukhriyyan' takes a kasra or damma; these are linguistic and recitation points that do not change the general sense.

God tells His Prophet to say to the idolaters of Quraysh that he is only a warner, and that there is no deity worthy of worship but God, the One, the Subduer, Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever lies between them, the Mighty who cannot be resisted, and the Oft-Forgiving toward those who turn back to Him. The commentators agree on the general sense: affirming monotheism and God's lordship, while recalling that He overpowers all things and forgives whoever returns to Him. Al-Razi sees a deliberate order, with the attribute of dominance mentioned first to frighten the indifferent, followed by the attributes of lordship, might and forgiveness to encourage them, and he explains that dominance proves God's oneness while forgiveness shows His mercy. Ibn 'Ashur argues that mentioning the Forgiver after the Subduer keeps the idolaters from despairing of repentance, a point close to al-Sa'di, who ties dominance to oneness. Opinions differ on the 'mighty tidings': Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the Quran, others understand the Day of Resurrection, and most keep the Quran and the accounts it contains. Several commentators then mention the dispute among the exalted angels about Adam; Ibn 'Abbas relates it to the creation of Adam, while Ibn Kathir and others cite a report about expiations and ranks, which Ibn Kathir distinguishes from the dispute mentioned in the Quran. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain the divine names as a might that cannot be overcome and a pardon that covers the sins of His servants.

God tells His Prophet to say to his people that the Qur'an is a momentous report, and that they turn away from it heedlessly. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Shurayh, identify this report as the Qur'an, while al-Hasan links it to the Day of Resurrection and al-Zamakhshari takes it as the story of Adam's creation, known without any human instruction. Ibn Atiyya sees it as the whole content of revelation on monotheism and the afterlife. As for the "exalted assembly", the majority identify it as the angels, whose dispute concerned Adam when God announced that He would place a successor on earth, as Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Qatada explain. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi also cite the hadith about expiations and degrees, which al-Tirmidhi graded as sound, but Ibn Kathir holds that this hadith is not the dispute mentioned in the Qur'an. Abu Hayyan reports a different view that the dispute concerned the unbelieving Arabs and the angels. Readers differ on "innama": most read it with a fatha, while Abu Ja'far reads it with a kasra as a quoted statement. The commentators stress that the passage proves the truth of the message, since the Prophet could not have known such matters on his own.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to the disbelievers that the Quran is a momentous report, and it rebukes them for turning away from it, neither reflecting on it nor acting by it. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi, al-Jalalayn, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur, take the report to be the Quran itself. Al-Hasan reads it as the Day of Judgment and Qatada as resurrection after death, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the story of Adam known only through revelation. Commentators differ on what turning away means: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as denying the message, while al-Sam'ani takes it as being heedless of it and abandoning it. The next verse says the Prophet had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when it disputed. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand this as the angels' dispute about Adam when God announced a successor on earth. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith about expiations and degrees as an account of the angels' dispute, though al-Qurtubi notes its chain is weak. Al-Zamakhshari holds that God spoke through an intermediary angel, and Abu Hayyan explains the dispute as a verbal exchange. Nearly all conclude that this knowledge came only by revelation, which proves the Prophet's truthfulness. Al-Razi adds that the dispute concerned whether creating humans, who could be swayed by desire and anger, was worthwhile.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to declare to his people that he had no knowledge of the Highest Assembly, the angels, when they disputed, and that his knowledge of this account comes only through revelation, so he is only a clear warner. Most commentators, from Ibn 'Abbas through Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, identify the Highest Assembly as the angels, and their dispute as the one about Adam, when God said He would place a khalifa on earth and they replied, will You place in it one who causes corruption and sheds blood?

Opinions differ on other points. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi take the great news to be the Qur'an, al-Hasan takes it to be the Day of Resurrection, and others take it to be the story of Adam.
