Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite a hadith about the Highest Assembly disputing over expiations and degrees, which Ibn Kathir grades as sound, while noting it is not the dispute mentioned in the Qur'an. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari place the exchange among the angels, Adam and Iblis. On the reading 'innama' with a kasra, al-Tabari, al-Farra' and Ibn al-Jawzi treat it as quoted speech, meaning only this statement: I am a clear warner.

This verse states that the Prophet ﷺ had no knowledge of his own of the dispute of the highest assembly, and that what is revealed to him is only a clear warning. The commentators agree that the 'highest assembly' refers to the angels, and that their dispute concerned Adam and his being made a khalifa on earth, as in the words 'Will You place upon it one who will spread corruption?' Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada report this meaning, while al-Hasan held that the angels claimed to be more noble and more knowledgeable than any future creation. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi cite the hadith of the dream in which the Prophet is asked about the dispute over expiations and degrees, though Ibn Kathir holds that this is not the dispute mentioned in the Quran. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan suggest the exchange took place through an intermediary angel, so the disputants are the angels, Adam and Iblis. The word 'nabaʾ' is taken by al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas to mean the Quran, while others read it as the Day of Judgement or the story of Adam. Abu Ja'far reads 'innama' with a kasra as a quoted statement, whereas the majority reading with a fatha implies a restriction of the mission to warning. Al-Razi links the passage to the affirmation of God's oneness, and Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a proof of revelation.

God instructs His Prophet to tell his people that the exalted assembly had knowledge of the account of Adam's creation, when the Lord told the angels that He would create a human from clay, and that once He had shaped him and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to fall prostrate before him. The commentators agree that "basharan" refers to Adam, that breathing in the spirit is an expression of honour, and that the prostration was one of greeting and reverence rather than worship, which belongs to God alone. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that all the angels prostrated except Iblis, who was proud and thereby became one of the disbelievers; al-Tabari explains this as known in God's foreknowledge, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take his disbelief to have occurred at that moment of refusal. Mujahid reads the "hand" as emphasis, others as power, while al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it as a real attribute that does not resemble the hands of creatures. As for the dispute mentioned in the verse, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Mawardi differ: some say it was the angels' question about who would spread corruption on earth, others that they claimed they were nobler and more knowledgeable, and others mention expiations and degrees of rank. Al-Razi draws from the story a lesson against envy and arrogance, the causes of Iblis's ruin and of the Quraysh's rejection of the Prophet. The commentaries agree that the verse affirms that what the Prophet relates of the unseen comes only by revelation from God.

This passage tells how God informed the angels that He would create a human from clay, and that once He had perfected him and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to fall prostrate before him. The commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, agree that this refers to Adam and that the phrase "of My spirit" is a mark of honour. Most understand the breathing as the bestowal of life rather than a physical breath. They agree that all the angels prostrated except Iblis, who was arrogant and became one of the disbelievers. They differ on the meaning of the last point: Ibn Abbas and those who follow him take it as disbelief known to God in advance, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as actual disbelief at the moment of refusal. Most hold that the prostration was one of greeting and honour rather than worship, al-Nasafi describing it as a bowing or a prostration to God, while Ibn Ashur notes that pride and envy were already latent in Iblis. For al-Razi, the story warns against envy and arrogance, the vices that moved Iblis and later the Meccan opponents of the Prophet. On the word "hands" in "created with My two hands", Mujahid reads it as emphasis, others as power, and al-Shawkani as two attributes of the divine essence.

This passage of Surah Sad recounts that God told the angels He would create a human from clay, and that once He had shaped him and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to prostrate to him. The commentators agree that this human is Adam, that breathing in the spirit means bringing him to life and giving him sensation, and that ascribing the spirit to God honours Adam. On the phrase 'by My hand', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to direct creation and honour, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that God personally undertook the creation, and some take it as a real attribute of God without likening it to creatures. All agree that the angels, every one of them, prostrated in obedience to God's command, and that the words 'all' and 'together' express totality and simultaneity. Only Iblis refused, out of arrogance. On the meaning of 'and he was among the disbelievers', Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya take it as God's foreknowledge of his disbelief, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan understand that he became a disbeliever at the moment of refusal. Some hold that the prostration was a greeting rather than worship, and was permitted before being abrogated. The story serves here as a warning against pride and envy, since Iblis considered himself better than Adam because he was made of fire, and was cast out. The commentators also mention the respite granted to Iblis until the appointed day and his oath 'by Your might'. The passage ends with the command to the Prophet to declare that he is only a warner who asks no wage and claims nothing beyond his mission, that the Quran is a reminder to all worlds, and that its news will be known after a time.

This passage of Surah Sad recounts that God told the angels He would create a human from clay, and that once He had shaped him and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to prostrate to him. All of them prostrated except Iblis, who was arrogant and became one of the disbelievers. The commentators agree that this prostration was one of honour and obedience rather than worship, and that pride was the reason for his refusal. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Iblis claimed he was better than Adam, since he was created from fire and Adam from clay, a faulty analogy that led him to disbelief. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that God expelled him and granted him respite until the appointed time. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that his disbelief arose at the moment of refusal, while others take the phrase to mean that he was a disbeliever in God's foreknowledge.

Opinions differ on several words. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi explain 'with My hands' as meaning power or care, al-Razi sees the breathing of the spirit as an honour granted to Adam, and al-Qurtubi regards the attribution of the spirit to God as a mark of distinction. Ibn 'Uthaymin affirms that God has two real hands that do not resemble those of creatures, a position al-Tabari's commentary does not adopt. On Iblis's nature, some say he was among the jinn who lived among the angels, which explains why the address concerns him.

The commentators agree that the story warns against pride and envy, which led to Iblis's fall and which are also reflected in the unbelievers' rejection of the message. They debate whether the exception is continuous or discontinuous.

This passage of Surah Sad recounts God's exchange with Iblis after he refused to prostrate to Adam when commanded. God asks him what prevented him: is it arrogance now, or was he already among the haughty? The commentators agree that this question is a rebuke, and that the phrase 'what I created with My two hands' honours Adam and shows God's special care for His creation. On the meaning of the two hands, the scholars differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the early scholars affirm them as a divine attribute in a manner befitting God, as do the Jalalayn and Ibn Uthaymin. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and others read them as power or blessing. Ibn Juzayy regards the verse as one of the ambiguous passages to be believed without fixing its nature. Al-Razi argues at length against anthropomorphism, and Ibn al-Qayyim draws on the differing grammatical forms of the word 'hand'. Iblis reasoned by analogy that he is better than Adam because he was made of fire and Adam of clay. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur consider this reasoning flawed, since clay sustains life while fire destroys. On Iblis's nature, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir treat him as close to the angels, whereas Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Uthaymin rely on the verse of the Cave to call him a jinn, explaining that the command addressed to the angels still included him. All agree that he was cursed until the Day of Judgement and granted a respite, but they differ on its end: the first blast of the trumpet or the Day of Resurrection. The passage closes with the Prophet being told to say that he asks no wage for his message, that he is no pretender, that the Quran is a reminder to all worlds, and that its news will be known after a time, which scholars variously place at death, at the Resurrection, or at the battle of Badr.

This passage records Iblis's answer when God asked why he refused to prostrate before Adam: he claimed to be better than Adam because he was created from fire and Adam from clay. The commentators agree that this is a flawed analogy and an unfounded claim, since fire is not superior to clay and excellence depends on God's choice. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see in his refusal a pride against God's command, and read in it a warning to the pagans who rejected the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari discusses the question of whether angels or humans are superior, a point on which the schools differ, and explains that the real fault lay in Iblis relying on his own origin instead of obeying. Al-Razi rejects reading the hand as power or favour and holds it to be a real attribute of God, while Ibn al-Qayyim stresses that the mention of two hands signals the honour given to Adam. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the Arabs also use hand to mean power, and that Iblis erred in his analogy, since substances are alike and virtues come from divine choice. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi observe that Adam's honour also lies in his form, in the breathing of the spirit into him, and in his purpose, not in matter alone. Ibn Kathir concludes that Iblis was cast out and granted respite until an appointed time.

This verse records God's command to Iblis to leave the garden after he refused to prostrate to Adam, grew arrogant and claimed to be better than him. God calls him "rajim", which the commentators gloss as stoned, cast out and driven away. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, al-Sa'di, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi agree that the word means accursed and banished from mercy, and that the curse remains upon him until the Day of Judgment. They differ on where he is sent out from. Most say the Garden, others say the heavens, while al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliya understand it as the very form he had been given. Al-Baghawi cites al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl that because Iblis took pride in his creation, God changed it, so that his appearance turned dark after being bright and his beauty became ugly. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report the same account. On the meaning of "rajim", al-Alusi notes that it may refer to expulsion, to being pelted with stones, or to abasement. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the curse applies first in this world, and that the Day of Judgment, with its greater torment, will make that curse seem forgotten. Ibn 'Ashur observes that setting the Day of Judgment as the limit of the curse indicates its continuance throughout this life, and does not imply that it ends afterwards. God knows best.

The commentators explain that God told Iblis to leave, called him rajim, meaning stoned, expelled and cursed, and informed him that the curse would be upon him until the Day of Judgment. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi, agree on this meaning of the word. They differ on where he is to leave: the Garden for most, the heavens for others, and for al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya the state of being he was in; al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl reports that God changed his form, so that it became black and ugly. As for the limit set to the curse, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that it does not mean it ends on that day, but that the punishment that follows will make him forget the curse. Ibn 'Ashur takes it to mean a duration covering the whole of worldly life, while al-Alusi and al-Qasimi see it as an illustration of what awaits him. Regarding the respite Iblis requested, Ibn Kathir and most scholars take it to be the Day of Resurrection, while others understand it as the moment of his death, or his death at Badr according to some. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Abi Hatim report that most consider him still alive, an opinion al-Tabari judges the more correct.

This verse records that Iblis, after being cast out and cursed until the Day of Judgment, asked his Lord to grant him respite until the day when people are raised from their graves. The commentators agree that he sought a delay and not to be destroyed. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn explain that he wanted to be spared until the resurrection. Ibn Kathir adds that the Forbearing granted him the delay without hastening him, and that once he felt safe from destruction he became defiant and arrogant. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi say he wanted room to lead mankind astray, to take revenge on them, and to escape death himself, since there is no death after the resurrection. Al-Alusi suggests he may have known this through reason or through what he had heard from the angels.

The divine reply is understood in the same general way, but the meaning of the "appointed time" divides the exegetes. The majority, as Ibn 'Atiyya reports, holds that he was granted respite until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean the time of the first blast of the trumpet. Another view, also reported by Ibn 'Atiyya, holds that he did not get what he asked for and received only a respite until the moment he himself would die, and some add that he died on the day of Badr. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di note that this delay served a divine wisdom, since without Iblis disobedience would vanish and concepts such as faith, jihad and enjoining good would lose their meaning.

Finally, according to Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, Iblis does not ask for repentance or relief, but only for a delay in which to pursue his enmity.

In this verse God grants Iblis his request for respite: he is among those who are reprieved until the appointed day, the known time. The commentators agree on the general sense: this is the term God set for the end of all creatures. They differ on what this appointed time is. Most, including Ibn Kathir, al-Samʿani, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn ʿAtiyya, take it to be the first blast of the Trumpet, when all creatures die. Al-Hasan and Ibn ʿAbbas understand it as the Day of Resurrection, the time of reckoning. Al-Qurtubi reports that Iblis had asked to be spared until the day of resurrection in order to escape death, but that his request was answered in a way that defeated his purpose. Ibn ʿAtiyya notes that the majority hold that Iblis was granted his respite and is still alive, while another group says he did not get what he asked for and will die at the time set for his death, and some add that he died at Badr. Al-Zamakhshari explains that this moment is known only to God and can be neither advanced nor delayed. Ibn ʿAshur observes that the answer follows what was decreed from eternity. Al-Alusi holds that the respite is not a special favour but follows from divine wisdom, and al-Qasimi sees in this moment the Great Resurrection. All the commentators agree that the answer reflects God's wisdom and is not an indulgence towards Iblis.

The commentators explain that God's words "until the day of the appointed time" answer Iblis's request to be reprieved until the Resurrection. He is granted a term fixed by God, which will be neither advanced nor delayed. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani, identify this time with the first blast of the trumpet, when all creatures die. Others, such as Ibn Juzayy and the Jalalayn, simply take it to mean the Day of Judgement. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report the majority view that Iblis did not receive what he asked for, but a respite that ends with his own death; some say he died on the day of Badr. Al-Razi notes that Iblis's aim was to escape death, and that only God knows the term. Al-Sam'ani and Ibn 'Ashur follow the same line, while al-Sa'di understands it as the moment when the offspring is complete and the trial is over. Abu al-Su'ud adds that the particle "fa" links the announcement of the term to the request rather than granting the request itself.

This verse from Surah Sad records Iblis swearing by the might of God, meaning His power and dominion, that he will lead astray all the children of Adam except the sincere servants of God. Most commentators take the particle ba as a particle of oath, while some allow that it may carry the sense of seeking help. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that Iblis knew he had no might of his own, and so he swore by God's. Al-Tabari explains that misguidance here means leading into error, and that sincerity is what God uses to protect a servant from Iblis's seduction. Al-Qurtubi understands misguidance as calling people to sins and making them appealing. Ibn Kathir links the exceptions to God's words that He gives Iblis no power over His servants. Al-Razi reports that the word for misguiding is sometimes attributed to the human being, in a reading close to free will, and sometimes to God, in a reading close to predestination, and he concludes that he is undecided on this question; this reading is particular to him. As for the word sincere, readings differ: some take it as those whom God has chosen, and others as those who devoted their worship to God alone. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that God granted Iblis respite until the appointed time, which is the first blast of the trumpet. The commentators agree that Iblis cannot lead the sincere astray, but they differ on the precise meaning of sincerity. The verses that follow in the surah concern the truth of the revelation, and the exegetes do not settle their differences on that point.

This passage reports that Iblis, having been granted respite until the appointed day, swore by God's might that he would mislead all the children of Adam except the sincere servants whom God has purified for Himself and protected from misguidance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that these "sincere" ones are those God has chosen for His worship and kept from seduction, so that most people are open to misleading while the sincere escape it. Ibn al-Qayyim adds that whoever takes refuge in God, sincerely devotes himself to Him and relies on Him has no power over him from Satan, whose authority extends only over those who take him as an ally and associate others with God. Al-Razi notes the question of whether misguidance is attributed to oneself or to God without deciding between them.

Commentators differ on the meaning of the oath "by Your might". Al-Zamakhshari takes it as an oath by God's dominion and power, while Ibn Atiyya reports Qatada's view that Iblis, knowing he had no might of his own, swore by God's might. As for God's words "The truth, and the truth I speak", Asim and Hamza read the first word in the nominative and the others in the accusative, and Mujahid explains it as "I am the Truth"; al-Baghawi treats it as an oath. Several scholars understand the "mutakallifin" as those who speak from their own initiative. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that some considered this verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, a view he rejects, while most do not regard it as abrogated. On the phrase "after a time", the opinions point to death, the Day of Judgment, or the battle of Badr.

The commentators explain that this verse is God's answer to Iblis, who had sworn by His might that he would mislead the children of Adam. God declares that the truth is from Him and that He speaks only the truth, and that He will fill Hell with you and with those among mankind who follow you, all of them. Most agree that these words are God's, but the grammar of the two words al-haqq divides the readers: Asim and Hamza read the first in the nominative and the second in the accusative, while the others read both in the accusative. Mujahid and Ibn Abbas understand it as 'I am the Truth and I speak the truth', or 'the truth is from Me'. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report other readings: an oath sworn by the Truth, meaning God; an imperative 'hold to the truth'; or an absolute object meaning 'truly'. Al-Farra takes it to mean 'in truth'. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya see 'and I speak only the truth' as a parenthesis between the oath and its answer. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that al-haqq may be a divine name or the opposite of falsehood. On 'minka', al-Zamakhshari reads it as the jinn and 'those who follow you' as the human descendants of Adam; Abu Hayyan takes 'ajma'in' as an emphasis on the pronoun. Ibn Kathir compares this verse with 32:13.

The commentators explain that this verse comes in the exchange between God and Iblis, after Iblis refused to prostrate before Adam and asked for respite. God's reply affirms a solemn truth: He will fill Hell with Iblis and with all of Adam's descendants who follow him, without exception. Mujahid and Ibn Abbas read the phrase "fa-l-haqqu wa-l-haqqa aqulu" as "I am the Truth, and I speak the truth" or "the truth is from Me and My word is true." Al-Suddi takes it as an oath God swears. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that "haqq" may refer to God's name or simply to the opposite of falsehood. The readers Asim, Hamza and Khalaf read the first word in the nominative and the rest in the accusative, and grammarians debated these forms, some seeing an exhortation to follow the truth, others an oath, others a sense of "indeed." As for "minka," most take it to mean the jinn, of Iblis's kind, while "mimman tabi'aka minhum" refers to humans descended from Adam. Al-Zamakhshari allows that "ajma'in" may emphasise either the followers and those they followed together, or the descendants of Adam alone. Ibn Kathir links the passage to similar threats in Surat al-Sajda and Surat al-Isra. The commentators do not settle these readings in a single conclusion.

The plain meaning of the verse is that God tells His Prophet ﷺ to say to the idolaters that he asks no wage from them for conveying the Quran, and that he is not among those who force themselves to speak or invent what God has not revealed. The commentators agree that the pronoun "it" refers to the Quran, the revelation or the message, and that the point is to deny any desire for worldly gain or status. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd take the sense to be about the Quran itself, which contains no contrivance or fabrication. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya widen the idea of artifice to include claiming knowledge or qualities one does not have, and Ibn Mas'ud, cited by al-Qurtubi, links the verse to the wisdom of saying "God knows best" about what one does not know. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl holds that this verse abrogates the verse on love for the kin of the Prophet, but Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy do not accept this. Al-Tabari understands the wage to be a reward in this world. The end of the passage says the Quran is a reminder to all the worlds and that people will come to know the truth of its message after a time. Opinions differ on this delay: Qatada and Ibn Abbas say it is death, Ikrima says the Day of Resurrection, al-Suddi says the battle of Badr, and al-Hasan says the moment of death. Ibn Kathir considers these views complementary rather than contradictory. The Prophet ﷺ conveyed only what he was commanded, adding nothing and leaving nothing out.

This verse states that the Qur'an is only a reminder and an admonition for all creatures, both humans and jinn, as the commentators explain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take "the worlds" to mean the two rational kinds of beings, humans and jinn, a reading Ibn 'Abbas also supports. Al-Jalalayn specifies that the address is to humans, jinn and rational beings, excluding the angels, while Ibn Sa'di, al-Alusi and others widen the sense to any being able to understand according to its capacity. The reminder, they say, guides each person toward what benefits them in religion and in worldly life.

The second part, "you will know its news after a while," has been understood in several ways. Qatada, Ibn Kathir and others take it to mean death, while Ikrima, Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas refer to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Sudi applies it to the battle of Badr, and al-Hasan notes that certainty comes at the moment of death. Al-Tabari holds that the text fixes no particular duration, since the Arabs did not limit the word hin to a set period, so the term should be left open. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the truth of the Qur'an becomes evident both in this world and in the hereafter, covering both warning and promise.

No commentator draws a legal ruling from this verse. Al-Razi links it to the proofs given earlier in the surah, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as the closing statement of Surah Sad.

The commentators explain that God commands His Prophet to tell the polytheists that the Quran is only a reminder and admonition for all beings, humans and jinn alike, that he asks no wage for it, and that he does not invent what is not his. The verse closes with a warning: they will come to know the truth of the Quran's report, its promises and threats, after a time. The exegetes agree that the 'report' refers to the truth of the Quran and the reality of what it announces, and the threat in the verse is clear. As for the word 'hin' (a time), they differ on its duration. Qatada and al-Hasan, reported by al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi, and Ibn Abbas according to some transmissions, take it to mean death, when the certain news comes to a person. Ibn Zayd and Ikrima take it to mean the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Zayd linking the verse to the final abode where truth is established and falsehood perishes. As-Suddi takes it to mean the Battle of Badr, when the disbelievers recognised by the sword the truth of the Quranic threat, a view Ibn Kathir also adopts. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Juzayy report that those who lived saw Islam rise, while those who died knew after death. At-Tabari holds that the Arabs set no fixed limit to hin, so it should not be confined to a single moment. Ikrima distinguishes a hin that can be reached from one that cannot, as in the verse about the palm tree. Several commentators read the verse as a threat, and al-Razi sees it as a fitting conclusion to the proofs presented earlier.
